# der, die, das

Every German noun has a **grammatical gender**: masculine, feminine or neuter. You can see it in the article that comes before the noun. In English all three are simply *the*.

| Gender | Article | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Masculine | `der` | `der Tisch` | the table |
| Feminine | `die` | `die Lampe` | the lamp |
| Neuter | `das` | `das Buch` | the book |

The gender belongs to the **word**, not to the thing. A table isn't male in any real sense, and `das Mädchen` (the girl) is neuter.

> **The colour code in this course:** masculine nouns are shown in blue, feminine in red and neuter in green. You'll see it in the answers of the vocabulary exercises.

## Learn every noun with its article

There is no rule that predicts the gender of every noun, so treat the article as part of the word. Don't learn `Tisch`, learn `der Tisch`. That's why the vocabulary exercises only accept a noun together with its article.

## Endings that help

Some endings almost always tell you the gender:

- **Feminine:** nouns ending in *-ung*, *-heit*, *-keit*, *-schaft*, *-ion* and *-tät*: `die Wohnung`, `die Freiheit`, `die Freundschaft`, `die Station`
- **Neuter:** small things ending in *-chen* or *-lein*: `das Brötchen`, `das Häuschen`. This is why `das Mädchen` is neuter.
- **Masculine:** days, months and seasons: `der Montag`, `der Mai`, `der Sommer`

## Plural: always die

In the plural, every noun uses `die`, whatever its gender:

| Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- |
| `der Tisch` | `die Tische` |
| `die Lampe` | `die Lampen` |
| `das Buch` | `die Bücher` |

So `die` alone doesn't tell you the gender. `die Bücher` is plural, but `das Buch` is neuter.

## In short

1. Every noun is masculine (`der`), feminine (`die`) or neuter (`das`).
2. Learn each noun together with its article.
3. Endings like *-ung* (feminine) and *-chen* (neuter) are reliable clues.
4. All plurals use `die`.
